sections.content: How many people stayed in Cambridge after gaining qualifications?

Cambridge is a large town in the East of England. Cambridge also has a university.

Cambridge has lower levels of deprivation.

Overall, Cambridge ended up with:

  • more graduates than it produced
  • more non-graduates with advanced qualifications than it produced
Note: all towns and cities in this analysis are defined based on population size only. This means that some cities are classed as towns because of their population.

Let's explore this further

There were 3,835 state-school pupils from Cambridge who sat their GCSEs between the 2007 to 2008 and the 2010 to 2011 school years.

Of these, 1,560 (41%) went on to gain degree-level qualifications (level 6+ as defined by The Office of Qualifications and Examinations Regulation, or Ofqual ). We will call these people graduates.

Another 955 (25%) went on to gain other advanced post-16 qualifications, such as A-Levels, a foundation degree or higher apprenticeship (levels 3-5 as defined by Ofqual). In this tool, we will refer to these non-graduates with advanced qualifications as “qualified non-graduates", for brevity.

The charts below compare Cambridge to other English towns and cities using three measures:

  • what proportion of Cambridge's pupils became graduates or qualified non-graduates by the 2017 to 2018 academic year
  • of those graduates and qualified non-graduates, the percentages that lived in Cambridge in the 2018 to 2019 academic year
  • how many graduates and qualified non-graduates from elsewhere came to live there by 2018 to 2019, relative to the number who sat their GCSEs there

In some towns, some of this information may not be available because of small sample sizes.
The size and deprivation level of a town, as well as the qualification levels of older residents, were all related to students' educational attainment. Read our previous analysis.

Where did those who left Cambridge move to?

Of Cambridge's graduates, 580 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 95 of those graduates (16%) were living fairly locally, in the Cambridge travel to work area (TTWA).

Of Cambridge's qualified (level 3+) non-graduates, 285 were living elsewhere in 2018/19.

However, 135 of those qualified non-graduates (47%) were living fairly locally, in the Cambridge travel to work area (TTWA).

Of those in Cambridge's GCSE cohort:

  • 445 graduates left the East of England
  • the most common region they moved to was London
  • 100 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates left the East of England
  • the most common region they moved to was London

In 2018 to 2019, 69% of graduates and 43% of qualified non-graduates living in Cambridge had moved there from elsewhere

In the 2018 to 2019 academic year, there were 3,045 graduates and 1,135 qualified (level 3+) non-graduates from our cohort living in Cambridge. This is compared with the 1,560 graduates and 955 qualified non-graduates who had lived there when they sat their GCSEs.

In 2018 to 2019, 31% of the graduates had also lived in Cambridge as GCSE pupils, while 69% had moved there from elsewhere.

Of the qualified non-graduates who lived in Cambridge in 2018 to 2019, 57% had lived there as GCSE pupils, while 43% had moved to the area from elsewhere.
